headline: Stellwagen edge in 130 feet: haddock thick on the mud, bluefin still working the Basin line
subhead: Groundfish split the bank by bottom type this week while school bluefin held tight to bait pushed up against the Basin drop.
body_markdown:
Eighty feet on the gravel, one-thirty on the mud, and a temperature break sitting right along the Stellwagen Edge where the bank falls into the Basin — that's the three-number summary of the week, and it explains most of what the fleet found and didn't find. Southwest wind held in the 8-12 knot range through most of the stretch, which is about as good as August gives you out here, and it kept the bank fishable four out of six days. The one blow that mattered came through on a weekday and scattered bait for about eighteen hours before things settled back down. That matters more than it sounds like, because both the groundfish and the tuna are following forage right now, not just structure.

Cod have been a scratch fishery on the gravel patches, the way they usually are in late August. Boats working the classic hard-bottom stretches on the northwest corner found fish in the 80 to 100-foot range, but you had to move to find them — jigging diamond jigs and Norwegian-style bucktails tipped with clam wasn't producing steady drifts, it was producing one or two keepers per good mark and a lot of marks with nothing on them. That's normal for this time of year. The cod aren't schooled up tight like they will be come November; they're spread thin over structure, sitting in the cooler pockets where the gravel breaks up the bottom current.

Haddock is where the real consistency has been. The mud bottom in that 110 to 140-foot band, particularly toward the deeper flats south of the main bank, has been holding fish willing to eat. Standard haddock rigs — two-hook bottom rigs with green or chartreuse tube teasers ahead of a clam or squid strip — have been putting decent numbers of keeper haddock in the box on the drift, especially on the last of the ebb when the current slows enough to fish straight up and down instead of getting blown sideways. Boats that worked the mud methodically, marking soft returns just off bottom and repositioning rather than sitting on one spot, did noticeably better than anyone who anchored and waited. Haddock this year have been mobile, and the mud isn't uniform — there are richer patches and dead patches within a few hundred yards of each other.

Bluefin have been the story worth calling ahead about. We flagged last week that the surface activity on the bank would likely hold as long as bait didn't scatter, and that's essentially what played out — the one wind event did knock things back for the better part of a day, but the school bluefin regrouped on the mackerel pushed up tight against the Stellwagen Edge and along the drop into the Basin. These are school-class fish, not giants, working bait balls close enough to the surface that jigging and casting have both been productive when boats can get on top of them without spooking the school. Green machines and small metal jigs worked fast through the upper thirty feet have drawn strikes, and where the fish were feeding hard on the surface, stickbaits and poppers cast into the boils did their job too. The pattern has been classic mackerel-driven bluefin behavior — tight to bait, moving with it, here one hour and a half mile away the next. Boats spending time scouting birds and bait showers before committing to a stop are the ones connecting; running straight to yesterday's numbers has been a mixed bag.

There's a secondary piece worth mentioning. The warm-water push that's been talked about around the Cape and Islands this month appears to be nudging a bit more life into these waters generally — nothing dramatic on the groundfish side, but the tuna activity has stayed livelier later into the season than a typical year, and that's consistent with a warmer regime holding offshore longer than usual. Whether that continues to bring anything unusual toward Tillies Bank or the approaches toward Carter Canyon and Cape Cod Tails remains to be seen, but it's the kind of signal worth watching if you're running that direction anyway for tuna or looking at fall groundfish prospects early.

Looking at the next few days, the wind pattern looks like it holds in a similar southwest groove, which should keep the bank fishable and keep the tuna bite from getting blown out. The moon is building toward full, and that typically sharpens tidal push on the bank — expect the haddock bite on the mud to concentrate into tighter windows around the tide changes rather than staying spread all day, so timing the drift to the last two hours of the ebb or the first two of the flood is the smarter play than fishing through the whole cycle. For cod, keep working the gravel edges methodically rather than committing to one mark; the fish are there but they're not schooled up enough yet to reward staying put. For bluefin, the call is the same as it's been — find the bait, not the boat you saw with fish yesterday. If the bait holds along the Stellwagen Edge and doesn't get pushed off by another wind event, the school bluefin bite should keep going through the week. If a front comes through and scatters the mackerel again, expect a day or two of hunting before things reset. Either way, worth having tackle rigged for both bottom fish and a surface pop before you leave the dock — this time of year on Stellwagen, you often need both in the same trip.
